problem:
Consider the curve defined parametrically as 

$$
x={e}^{t}-t,\,y=4{e}^{t/2},\,t\in [0,\operatorname{ln}⁡4].
$$

Determine the surface area $S$ generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis. Do not round the answer.

$S=$
{{field-1}}
worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi y\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=0$ to ${t}_{2}=\operatorname{ln}⁡4.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t}-t)={e}^{t}-1, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4{e}^{t/2})=2{e}^{t/2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}4{e}^{t/2}\sqrt{{({e}^{t}-1)}^{2}+{(2{e}^{t/2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}4{e}^{t/2}\sqrt{{e}^{2t}-2{e}^{t}+1+4{e}^{t}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}4{e}^{t/2}\sqrt{{e}^{2t}+2{e}^{t}+1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}4{e}^{t/2}\sqrt{({e}^{t}+1)^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}4{e}^{t/2}({e}^{t}+1)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}8\pi {e}^{t/2}({e}^{t}+1)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We evaluate the last integral using the substitution $u={e}^{t/2}.$ Then, $\text{d}u=\frac{1}{2}{e}^{t/2}\,\text{d}t,$ or $2\,\text{d}u={e}^{t/2}\,\text{d}t.$ We also update the limits of integration for $u:$

| **$t$** | $0$ | $\operatorname{ln}⁡4$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $1$ | $2$ |

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}S & ={\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}8\pi ({e}^{t}+1)\cdot {e}^{t/2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}8\pi ({u}^{2}+1)\cdot 2\,\text{d}u \\  & =16\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}({u}^{2}+1)\,\text{d}u \\  & =16\pi {[\frac{{u}^{3}}{3}+u]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =16\pi ((\frac{8}{3}+2)-(\frac{1}{3}+1)) \\  & =16\pi (\frac{14}{3}-\frac{4}{3}) \\  & =16\pi (\frac{10}{3}) \\  & =\frac{160\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}
$$
